pharm: Disease-modifying agent for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
quick: Take 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal (high-fat food reduces absorption)
Limited data; use only if clearly needed
Avoid - excreted in animal milk; not recommended
No specific adjustment; limited data, use with caution
Contraindicated with baseline transaminases over 5x ULN; caution otherwise
Avoid - increases risk of liver injury
Liver enzymes (ALT), CBC for neutropenia, respiratory symptoms (ILD)
summary: Riluzole is a benzothiazole that modulates glutamatergic neurotransmission and is the first agent shown to prolong survival/time to tracheostomy in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). It reduces presynaptic glutamate release and stabilises inactivated voltage-dependent sodium channels, limiting excitotoxic injury to motor neurons. Dosed at 50 mg twice daily on an empty stomach, its key safety concerns are dose-related hepatotoxicity (monitor ALT), neutropenia, and interstitial lung disease. It is a CYP1A2 substrate, so smoking and CYP1A2 modulators affect its levels.
indications: Treatment of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) to extend survival and/or time to tracheostomy

dosage.n: No additional benefit and more adverse effects above 100 mg/day; take on an empty stomach

dosage.d: 50 mg every 12 hours (equivalent dosing in suspension or oral film)
dosage.n: Useful for patients with dysphagia; same food-timing precautions

admin: Take at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal to avoid reduced absorption
Take doses 12 hours apart at the same times each day
For oral film/suspension follow product-specific administration instructions (helpful in dysphagia)
Obtain baseline ALT/AST before starting and monitor periodically
Counsel on smoking effect: smoking induces CYP1A2 and lowers riluzole levels
moa: Riluzole's neuroprotective action in ALS is attributed to reduction of glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity. It inhibits presynaptic release of glutamate, stabilises the inactivated state of voltage-dependent sodium channels, and interferes with intracellular events following excitatory amino-acid receptor activation. The net effect is decreased excitotoxic injury to motor neurons, though the precise mechanism of its survival benefit is not fully defined.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to riluzole or its components (including anaphylaxis/angioedema reactions)
Baseline liver transaminases greater than 5 times the upper limit of normal, or clinically significant liver disease
relative: History of hepatic disease or elevated transaminases
Neutropenia or risk factors for it
monitor: Respiratory symptoms suggesting interstitial lung disease

preg: There are limited human data. Animal studies showed adverse effects at high doses. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Riluzole or its metabolites are excreted in the milk of lactating animals; it is not known whether it passes into human milk. Because of potential serious adverse effects, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment.
renal: There is no specific dose adjustment defined for renal impairment and data are limited; use with caution. Riluzole is mainly cleared by hepatic metabolism.
hepatic: Riluzole is hepatically metabolised (CYP1A2) and is hepatotoxic. It is contraindicated when baseline transaminases exceed 5x ULN. In patients with elevated baseline liver enzymes, use with caution and monitor closely; discontinue if ALT rises markedly or jaundice/hepatic injury develops.

major: Strong CYP1A2 inhibitors (fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin) increase riluzole exposure and toxicity risk
Other hepatotoxic drugs - additive risk of liver injury
moderate: CYP1A2 inducers (omeprazole, rifampin, charcoal-broiled foods) decrease riluzole levels
Caffeine, theophylline, phenacetin and other CYP1A2 substrates may compete
minor: No clinically significant minor interactions established
interactions.food: High-fat meals reduce absorption (lower AUC and Cmax) - take on an empty stomach; charcoal-broiled foods may lower levels via CYP1A2 induction
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - chronic alcohol increases the risk of hepatotoxicity
interactions.diagnostics: Cigarette smoking induces CYP1A2 and lowers riluzole levels; consider smoking status when interpreting effect/tolerability

common: Decreased lung function, somnolence, oral hypoesthesia (numbness)
emergency: Acute dyspnea from interstitial lung disease

monitoring: ALT/AST before treatment, every month for the first 3 months, then every 3 months for the rest of the first year, and periodically thereafter
Complete blood count if febrile illness occurs (to detect neutropenia)
Respiratory symptoms (cough, dyspnea) - investigate for interstitial lung disease and stop if confirmed
counsel: Take one tablet twice a day, 12 hours apart, on an empty stomach (1 hour before or 2 hours after food)
Report fever or signs of infection promptly so your blood count can be checked
Report yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe tiredness (possible liver problems)
Report new cough or breathlessness, and avoid alcohol
Tell your doctor if you smoke or change your smoking habits, as this affects the drug's levels
pk: Survival benefit is a long-term effect; no acute symptomatic onset
Plasma peak approximately 1-1.5 hours after oral dosing
Store at 20-25 C (excursions 15-30 C permitted); protect from light; follow product-specific storage for suspension/film
pearls: Riluzole is the first drug shown to prolong survival/time to tracheostomy in ALS - it modestly slows disease, it does not cure or reverse it
Hepatotoxicity is the key monitoring concern: it is contraindicated when baseline ALT/AST exceeds 5x ULN, and ALT should be checked on a defined schedule
Watch for neutropenia (check CBC with any febrile illness) and interstitial lung disease (investigate new cough/dyspnea)
It is a CYP1A2 substrate: smoking and CYP1A2 inducers lower levels, while inhibitors like fluvoxamine/ciprofloxacin raise them
Take on an empty stomach - a high-fat meal markedly reduces absorption
missed: If you miss a dose, skip it and take the next dose at your usual scheduled time. Do not take two doses together to make up for a missed one. Keep doses 12 hours apart on an empty stomach.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited; expect exaggerated neurological effects (somnolence, encephalopathy) and possibly methemoglobinemia, along with risk of hepatic and hematologic toxicity. There is no specific antidote. Treat supportively with symptomatic care and monitoring; methylene blue may be considered for significant methemoglobinemia.
